name: Case report / case series
gist: A detailed account of one or a few unusual cases. Raises a signal or a hypothesis; can't test it.
example: MMWR, June 1981: Pneumocystis pneumonia in five young men in Los Angeles, the first published description of AIDS.

name: Cross-sectional survey
gist: Measure exposure and outcome in a sample at one moment. Estimates prevalence; can't show which came first.
example: National health interview surveys estimating smoking prevalence by age and region.

name: Ecological study
gist: Compare groups (countries, regions, years) using aggregate data. A cheap hypothesis generator; individual-level conclusions are a trap.
example: Messerli (2012): national chocolate consumption vs. Nobel laureates per capita.

name: Monitoring / surveillance
gist: Systematic, repeated measurement of the same quantity across time and place to detect trends and signals.
example: The Mauna Loa CO₂ record (since 1958); post-marketing drug-safety pharmacovigilance.

name: Prospective cohort
gist: Measure exposures in people before outcomes happen, then follow them forward. Shows temporal order and incidence.
example: The Framingham Heart Study (1948–), which gave us the very idea of 'risk factors'.

name: Retrospective cohort
gist: Reconstruct a cohort and its outcomes from existing records. Fast and cheap, but limited to what someone happened to record.
example: Occupational cohorts assembled from employment records, e.g. asbestos and shipyard workers.

name: Case–control study
gist: Start from people with the outcome (cases) and comparable people without it (controls); compare their past exposures.
example: Doll & Hill (1950): smoking histories of lung-cancer patients vs. other hospital patients.

name: Case-crossover
gist: Each case is their own control: compare exposure just before the event with the same person's exposure at other times.
example: Mittleman et al. (1993): heavy exertion as a trigger of heart attack within the hour.

name: Target trial emulation
gist: Write the protocol of the trial you wish you could run, then emulate it step by step in observational data.
example: Hernán & Robins' framework; emulated trials of statins and vaccines using health records.

name: Instrumental variable analysis
gist: Find a factor that nudges the exposure but affects the outcome only through it: a natural coin flip.
example: Angrist & Krueger (1991): quarter of birth, compulsory schooling and earnings.

name: Mendelian randomization
gist: Use genetic variants as instruments. Genes are shuffled at conception, so carriers mimic a lifelong randomized trial.
example: LDL-lowering gene variants and coronary heart disease across large genetic consortia.

name: Difference-in-differences
gist: Compare the change over time in a group that got an intervention with the change in a similar group that didn't.
example: Card & Krueger (1994): New Jersey's minimum-wage rise vs. neighbouring Pennsylvania.

name: Regression discontinuity
gist: When a rule assigns treatment at a cutoff, compare units just above and just below: nearly identical except for treatment.
example: Angrist & Lavy (1999): Maimonides' rule capping class size at 40 pupils.

name: Interrupted time series
gist: Many measurements before and after a dated intervention; test for a change in level or slope beyond the existing trend.
example: Hospital admissions for heart attacks before and after a public smoking ban.

name: Synthetic control
gist: Build a weighted 'twin' of one treated unit from untreated units that tracked it before the intervention; compare after.
example: Abadie et al.: California's 1988 tobacco programme; the economic cost of German reunification.

name: Randomized controlled trial
gist: Randomly allocate individuals to intervention or control, follow them up, compare outcomes. The benchmark for 'does it work?'
example: MRC streptomycin trial for tuberculosis (1948), the first modern randomized trial.

name: Cluster randomized trial
gist: Randomize whole groups (schools, clinics, villages) when the intervention acts at group level or would spill over.
example: School-based deworming and hygiene trials randomized by school.

name: Crossover trial
gist: Each participant gets both treatments in random order, separated by a washout. Needs far fewer people.
example: Bioequivalence studies of generic versus brand-name drugs.

name: Factorial experiment (DoE)
gist: Vary several factors at once in a controlled setting. Estimates each effect and their interactions in few runs.
example: Fisher's agricultural experiments at Rothamsted; screening designs in process engineering.

name: N-of-1 trial
gist: Repeated, randomized, ideally blinded treatment periods within a single patient to find out what works for them.
example: Personalized trials of pain or ADHD medication in individual patients.

name: Stepped-wedge trial
gist: All clusters start as controls and switch to the intervention at randomly ordered times until everyone has it.
example: The Gambia Hepatitis Intervention Study (1986), which phased in infant vaccination region by region.

name: Online A/B test
gist: Randomize users of a digital product to variants. Huge samples detect tiny effects within days.
example: Search and e-commerce platforms running thousands of controlled experiments a year.

name: Adaptive / platform trial
gist: One master protocol tests many treatments against a shared control; arms are dropped or added as data accrue.
example: RECOVERY (COVID-19): dexamethasone shown to save lives within about 100 days of launch.

name: Field experiment
gist: Manipulate a factor in the real world (plots, islands, villages, markets) with randomized replicates and controls.
example: Paine (1966, 1969): removing Pisaster starfish from a rocky shore collapsed its diversity: the 'keystone species'.

name: Ethnography
gist: Immerse yourself in a setting for months, observing and taking part, to understand practices and meanings from the inside.
example: Whyte's Street Corner Society (1943); Latour & Woolgar's Laboratory Life (1979).

name: Grounded theory
gist: Collect and analyse data in iterative cycles (coding, comparing, sampling) to build a new theory from the ground up.
example: Glaser & Strauss (1965), Awareness of Dying: how hospital staff and patients manage knowledge of death.

name: Interviews & thematic analysis
gist: In-depth interviews or focus groups analysed for patterns of meaning. Answers 'how' and 'why' from people's own view.
example: Exploring why patients stop taking a medication they were prescribed.

name: Case study (in-depth)
gist: Study one or a few bounded cases (a company, a project, a policy) in their real context, using many sources of evidence.
example: Allison's Essence of Decision (1971) on the Cuban missile crisis; engineering failure investigations.

name: Delphi consensus
gist: Experts rate statements anonymously over repeated rounds, seeing the group's feedback, until consensus emerges.
example: COMET-initiative 'core outcome sets' that tell trialists what every trial in a field should measure.

name: Mixed methods (sequential)
gist: Combine numbers and narratives in sequence: a survey then interviews to explain it, or interviews then a survey to test them.
example: Explanatory sequential design: a survey finds a gap, follow-up interviews explain it.

name: Systematic review & meta-analysis
gist: A pre-specified, exhaustive search and appraisal of all studies on a focused question; pool results where sensible.
example: Cochrane reviews; the antenatal-steroids forest plot in the Cochrane logo.

name: Scoping review
gist: Systematically map what research exists on a broad topic (concepts, methods, gaps) without pooling effects.
example: PRISMA-ScR guided maps, e.g. of how AI is used in nursing practice.

name: Network meta-analysis
gist: Compare many treatments at once by combining direct and indirect evidence across a network of trials.
example: Cipriani et al. (2018): 21 antidepressants ranked from 522 trials.

name: Umbrella review
gist: A review of systematic reviews: summarizes and grades the evidence across many reviews on a broad topic.
example: Theodoratou et al. (2014): vitamin D and 137 outcomes across meta-analyses and trials.

name: Rapid review
gist: A systematic review with transparently streamlined steps, delivered in weeks to inform an urgent decision.
example: Cochrane Rapid Reviews informing COVID-19 policy in 2020.

name: Realist review
gist: Synthesize mixed evidence to explain how complex programmes work: for whom, in what contexts, and why.
example: Pawson's realist syntheses of complex social programmes (context + mechanism → outcome).

name: Diagnostic accuracy study
gist: Apply a new test and a reference standard to consecutive people suspected of the condition; estimate sensitivity and specificity.
example: STARD-reported evaluations of rapid antigen tests against PCR.

name: Reliability & agreement study
gist: Repeat measurements across raters, occasions or devices; quantify agreement (kappa, ICC, Bland–Altman limits).
example: Bland & Altman (1986): why correlation is the wrong way to compare two measurement methods.

name: Instrument development & validation
gist: Build a questionnaire or scale from theory and input, then test its structure, reliability and validity (psychometrics).
example: Development of the Maslach Burnout Inventory (1981).

name: Interlaboratory comparison
gist: Identical samples go to many labs (a 'round robin'); differences reveal how reproducible a measurement method is.
example: Proficiency-testing schemes; BIPM key comparisons between national metrology institutes.

name: Analytical / mathematical theory
gist: Derive results from first principles with mathematics: proofs, closed-form solutions, bounds. 'What must be true if…'
example: Carnot's efficiency limit (1824); Nash equilibrium (1950).

name: Computational simulation
gist: Encode mechanisms in a model (FEM, CFD, Monte Carlo, agent-based) and run experiments impossible, dangerous or too costly in reality.
example: Numerical-relativity waveforms of black-hole mergers, computed years before LIGO's first detection.

name: Prediction model (statistical / ML)
gist: Develop a model that forecasts an outcome from predictors, then test its discrimination and calibration on new data.
example: The Framingham risk score; TRIPOD-reported clinical prediction models.

name: Design science (build & evaluate)
gist: Iteratively design an artifact (device, software, method) that solves a real problem, and evaluate it with users in context.
example: Usability-engineered medical devices (IEC 62366); research software built with its users.

name: Pilot / feasibility study
gist: A small rehearsal of a future study. Can we recruit, retain, deliver and measure? Not for estimating effects.
example: CONSORT extension for randomized pilot and feasibility trials (2016).

name: Benchmark evaluation
gist: Compare methods on shared tasks, datasets and metrics under identical conditions, with baselines, ablations and repeated runs.
example: ImageNet; robot-grasping benchmarks built on the YCB object set.
